title: Ohio State Edges Indiana After Marsh’s Out‑of‑Bounds Call Sparks Victory (ESPN)
body:
Ohio State clung to a 19‑15 victory over Indiana on Saturday night after a controversial call nullified what appeared to be a go‑ahead touchdown for the Hoosiers. With less than three minutes remaining, Indiana quarterback Julian Sayin connected on a 38‑yard strike to Jeremiah Smith on fourth‑and‑goal, only for officials to rule receiver’s left foot out of bounds. The reversal kept the Buckeyes ahead and secured their fourth straight win, preserving their No. 4 ranking in the College Football Playoff (CFP) poll.

The game, played at Indiana’s Memorial Stadium, was a defensive battle for most of its duration. Ohio State’s offense, led by senior quarterback C.J. Stroud, struggled to find rhythm against a disciplined Hoosier front seven that forced three sacks and limited the Buckeyes to just 225 total yards. Stroud’s most productive drive came in the second quarter, when he orchestrated a 12‑play, 68‑yard march that culminated in a 7‑yard touchdown run by running back Emeka Eze, giving Ohio State a 13‑7 lead at halftime. Indiana answered with a field goal before the break, but the Buckeyes’ special teams unit added a 38‑yard field goal in the third quarter, extending the margin to 16‑10.

The pivotal moment arrived early in the fourth quarter. After a three‑and‑out by Ohio State, Indiana drove 55 yards in just over two minutes, setting up a first‑and‑goal at the one‑yard line. Sayin, who had thrown for 215 yards and a touchdown up to that point, opted for a high‑risk, high‑reward play on fourth down. He lofted the ball toward the back corner of the end zone where Smith leapt and appeared to secure the ball before falling. The stadium erupted as the scoreboard flashed “TD,” but the officials convened quickly. After a brief review, they determined Smith’s left foot had touched the sideline before he completed the catch, rendering the play dead. The call sparked immediate protest from Indiana’s coaching staff and a heated debate among fans and analysts about the precision of the replay system.

Ohio State capitalized on the turnover, driving 45 yards in the ensuing possession. Stroud, who finished the night with 252 passing yards and two touchdowns, found tight end Noah Martinez on a 22‑yard pass that set up a decisive 23‑yard field goal by senior kicker Liam O’Connor. The successful kick pushed the lead to 19‑15, a margin the Buckeyes would protect for the remainder of the game. Indiana’s final drive stalled at the Ohio State 35‑yard line, where a sack on Sayin forced a fourth‑down attempt that fell incomplete, sealing the upset‑avoided result.

The outcome has significant implications for both programs. Ohio State remains firmly in the CFP conversation, holding onto the second spot in the Big Ten East and keeping its unbeaten streak alive at 5‑0. Coach Ryan Day praised his team’s resilience, noting, “We knew we had to finish strong, and the kids showed the composure to do that even when the call went against us.” Conversely, Indiana’s head coach Tom Allen expressed frustration but optimism, emphasizing the Hoosiers’ progress: “We fought hard, and those moments will build us. We’ll learn from the review and come back stronger.”

Analysts point to the controversial replay as a catalyst for ongoing discussions about the scope of instant‑review technology in college football. While the NCAA’s current guidelines require clear evidence to overturn a call, critics argue that the margin for error on boundary calls remains razor‑thin, often hinging on a single frame of video. The debate may prompt the conference to revisit its protocols before the season’s final stretch.

Looking ahead, Ohio State prepares for a pivotal matchup against Michigan State next week, a contest that could determine the Big Ten East champion. Indiana, meanwhile, returns home to face Purdue, where a win would keep their bowl aspirations alive. Both teams will carry the lessons learned from Saturday’s drama—Ohio State with the confidence of surviving a near‑collapse, and Indiana with the resolve to turn controversial setbacks into motivation for the remainder of the season.
